# R3 — Preparation (3:1–4:13) + Early Galilee (4:14–6:11)

**Range read in full:** raw 5593–6442 (slice ll. 1–850)  
**Source:** Joel B. Green, *The Gospel of Luke* (NICNT, 1997)  
**Scope:** §3 Preparation for the ministry of Jesus (3:1–4:13); §4.1–4.2 early Galilee (4:14–6:11) — John, baptism/genealogy/testing, Nazareth sermon, Capernaum, first disciples, table fellowship and Sabbath controversies.  
**Target slugs (when relevant):** [[luke]], [[joel-green]], [[jubilee]], [[jesus]], [[elijah]], [[elisha]], [[isaiah]], [[peter-apostle]]

## Claims

### C1 — Section 3:1–4:13 establishes probability of Jesus’ mission as Son of God
**Locus:** raw 5593–5636 (slice ll. 1–37)  
**Quote:** "Luke 1:5–2:52 may present the possibility of Jesus’ mission as Son of God but 3:1–4:13 establishes its probability—both by exhibiting how John prepared the way… and by narrating Jesus’ status transformation prior to his taking up his public ministry… (1) the completion of the narrative cycle concerning John… (2) that Jesus has been empowered for his mission by the Holy Spirit and has divine sanction; (3) that Jesus is appropriately credentialed… (4) that Jesus has discerned correctly the nature of his mission from God, in contradistinction to the counterfeit offered him by the devil; and (5) that Jesus has determined to embrace God’s purpose…"  
**Claim (Green):** For [[luke]], preparation is status actualization and competence-building for [[jesus]] as Son of God, not a new salvation-historical age; God remains primary actor; hostile forces (rulers, crowd, devil) threaten but the section assures Jesus will take up the mission.

### C2 — Birth–ministry thematic bridge: Spirit, Isaiah 40, universal reach, repentance
**Locus:** raw 5605–5623 (slice ll. 7–25)  
**Quote:** "• the programmatic use of Isaiah 40 (1:17, 19, 76; 3:4–6, 18); • the accent on the universalistic reach of God’s aim… • the role of John as one who prepares the way… • the activity of the Holy Spirit (1:15, 35, 41, 67; 2:25–27; 3:16, 22, 4:1); • repentance and forgiveness of sins… • conflict…"  
**Claim (Green):** 3:1–4:13 is continuous with 1:5–2:52; [[isaiah]] 40 is programmatic for John’s preparation; Spirit activity spans John, baptism, and testing.

### C3 — John removed “prematurely” so baptism centers Jesus alone; not two salvation ages
**Locus:** raw 5641–5645 (slice ll. 42–46)  
**Quote:** "it appears that he has removed John from the scene prematurely… Jesus was baptized, like the others, by John, but by the time of the narration of his baptism, John is unavailable… The separation of Jesus’ baptism from the others is dramatically motivated… These verses provide no basis for distinguishing the ministries of John and Jesus as belonging to two separate periods in salvation history."  
**Claim (Green):** Against Conzelmann-style periodization (implicit): Luke’s staging is dramatic, not dual-epoch; repentance/forgiveness and “good news” run John → Jesus → church (3:3; 4:18; 24:47; Acts 2:38).

### C4 — John as social-renewal prophet (OT form + wilderness/Jordan + Isa 40)
**Locus:** raw 5649–5653 (slice ll. 50–54)  
**Quote:** "John is portrayed by Luke as a prophet concerned with social renewal and transformation… introduction… reminiscent of the accounts of the prophets of Israel’s past… wilderness and the Jordan River… echo exodus and conquest themes… Luke’s interpretation of John’s appearance with the citation of Isa 40:3–5, suggesting that the promised eschatological deliverance of God’s people was imminent."  
**Claim (Green):** John is a renewal prophet in socio-political turmoil; religious roots “blossomed in socio-politico-economic justice”; different response of “all the people” vs. “Herod the ruler”; fruits of repentance = social justice (3:10–14).

### C5 — Josephus parallel (reported) and peasant “perceived deprivation”
**Locus:** raw 5650–5653 (slice ll. 51–54)  
**Quote:** "Josephus speaks of a number of renewal prophets, such as those during the rule of Felix (52–60 C.E.) who led the masses “… out into the wilderness so that God would show them signs of deliverance” (J.W. 2.13.4 §259)… In the moral economy of the peasant, perceived deprivation is tantamount to real deprivation…"  
**Claim (Green reporting/using Josephus + peasant moral economy):** John shares affinity with contemporary renewal movements; appeal rests on relative injustice among common folk, not absolute poverty.

### C6 — John’s repentance-baptism: social separation, passive submission, return as children of Abraham
**Locus:** raw 5655–5657 (slice ll. 56–58)  
**Quote:** "John’s primary interest is in calling people out of normal social existence in order to align themselves fundamentally with God’s eschatological, redemptive purpose… Through submitting to repentance-baptism, in which their roles were passive, they signified their surrender to God’s aim… By coming out into the wilderness… through baptism they embraced a conversion of loyalties… and in returning to their everyday lives they accepted the vocation to reflect behaviors apropos true children of Abraham."  
**Claim (Green):** Baptism is initiatory rite of passage (come out / undergo / return), not mere ritual purity analogue; forces crisis distinction between authentic Abraham’s children and outsiders; anticipates Spirit-and-fire baptism (Ezek 36:25–26).

### C7 — Water baptism vs Spirit-and-fire: not alternatives; Spirit + fire readings
**Locus:** raw 5658–5665, 6209–6224 (slice ll. 58–66, 210–224)  
**Quote:** "John’s baptism is not presented by Luke as an alternative to the baptism “with the Holy Spirit and fire.” Although the two are contrasted (3:16; cf. Acts 19:1–7), clearly the one anticipates and prepares for the other… Luke saw the full actualization of John’s promise in the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost… Another reading is possible… two baptisms—one with the Holy Spirit, one with fire… supported by Jesus’ announcement in 12:49…"  
**Claim (Green):** Preference leans toward Pentecost actualization of Spirit/fire as one baptism (Acts elliptical); alternative two-baptism (Spirit + judgment-fire) remains open via 12:49; either way John’s rite prepares Messiah’s work.

### C8 — 3:1–2 rulers list: tension-filled milieu, not mere dating; Tiberius/Pilate/Herod portraits
**Locus:** raw 5698–5709 (slice ll. 98–109)  
**Quote:** "concern with chronological specificity is for Luke clearly eclipsed by his interest in portraying the socio-historical climate… Luke’s synchronism in 3:1–2a provides… more than an historical setting… Rather, they bespeak a particular, tension-filled, top-heavy, socio-historical milieu."  
**Claim (Green):** List frames John vs. power elite; Pilate known for ferocity and for Jesus’ execution; Herod Antipas for Tiberias on unclean ground and for imprisoning John; Annas/Caiaphas singular “high priesthood” marks dynastic temple power (Acts 4:6); wilderness as new-exodus deliverance locale.

### C9 — Isa 40:3–5: not mere “fulfillment” but redemptive-historical location; “Lord” = Jesus
**Locus:** raw 5718–5721 (slice ll. 118–121)  
**Quote:** "Luke is not so concerned with presenting John as the “fulfillment” of this passage as he is in locating John… within this redemptive-historical context… By this point in the narrative, the original proposal that John’s ministry would prepare for the coming of Yahweh (1:17) has undergone a crucial shift. By “Lord” we now understand “Jesus”… Luke’s amendment… from “make straight the paths of our God” to “make his paths straight.” “His” now refers to the coming one—Jesus, the Lord."  
**Claim (Green):** Intertextual absorption of [[isaiah]] 40; christological shift of “Lord”; “way” seeds Acts absolute “the Way”; salvation universal (“all flesh”) though John’s mission narrower to Israel.

### C10 — Covenantal nomism repudiated; fruits of repentance decide covenant membership
**Locus:** raw 5723–5756, 6163–6169 (slice ll. 123–156, 163–169)  
**Quote:** "Such an understanding [E. P. Sanders’s covenantal nomism] is repudiated by John, who insists that children of Abraham are not identified by birth into the covenant community but through response to God’s gracious initiative… one’s relationship to the covenant at all is determined by engaging in behavior that brings the aim of God to expression… The eschatologically charged context… raises the stakes profoundly…"  
**Claim (Green, engaging Sanders):** John undercuts ethnic/covenant-birth security; “brood of vipers” vs. claim “We have Abraham as our father”; stones → new people (echo Isa 51:1–2; possible Gentile promise).

### C11 — Ethical fruits: share clothing/food; toll collectors keep prescribed amount; soldiers no extortion
**Locus:** raw 6191–6203 (slice ll. 191–203)  
**Quote:** "Whoever has two shirts must share with anyone who has none; and whoever has food must do likewise… Collect no more than the amount prescribed for you… Do not extort money from anyone by threats or false accusation, and be satisfied with your wages."  
**Claim (Green):** Ethics reach day-to-day local networks, not only large-scale injustice; not Greco-Roman bourgeois ethics but scriptural/wisdom with eschatological edge; “Even” toll collectors respond; no demand they abandon occupation—repentance within vocation; status-transposition trajectory for toll collectors.

### C12 — Messiah expectation fluid; John subordinates self; winnowing already done by John’s call
**Locus:** raw 6204–6230 (slice ll. 204–230)  
**Quote:** "hope is present but ill defined… the language John uses actually presumes that the process of winnowing has already been completed… John’s ministry of preparation is itself the winnowing… the role of the Messiah is portrayed as pronouncing or enacting judgment… John establishes an expectation for immediate judgment that is not actualized… he picks it up again in 7:18–20… and in 12:49…"  
**Claim (Green):** Messianic meaning shaped by contrast (status, Mal 3:1/4:5 messenger role, superior baptism); judgment timing becomes live narrative tension, not abandoned thread.

### C13 — John’s message = “good news”; imprisonment by Herod completes cycle / prefigures Jesus
**Locus:** raw 6231–6245 (slice ll. 231–245)  
**Quote:** "His preaching comes under the heading of “good news,” a description undoubtedly recommended to Luke by his presentation of John as the Isaianic herald… Herod lives in opposition to God, so it is only to be expected that he will oppose God’s spokesperson, John. If this is the lot of those who identify fundamentally with God’s redemptive aim… what will happen to the one for whom John’s ministry was a preparation?"  
**Claim (Green):** John finalized as Isaianic herald; Herod’s evil = justice/holiness infractions continuum with 3:10–14; opposition pattern for Jesus (and later church).

### C14 — Baptism scene centers Spirit endowment + divine sonship affirmation, not the dunking
**Locus:** raw 6253–6271 (slice ll. 253–271)  
**Quote:** "Luke is less interested in Jesus’ baptism as such, and more concerned with his endowment with the Spirit and God’s affirmation of his sonship… these actions are reported to have occurred not during Jesus’ baptism, but afterward, while he was praying… Thus, Jesus’ baptism as traditionally understood has been cast by the narrator as Jesus’ anointing by the Spirit… (1) sets in motion the sequence of events to follow… (2) is expounded as the event that determines his understanding of his divine mission and empowers him… (4:18–19; Acts 10:37–38); and (3) anticipates the analogous empowering of Jesus’ followers in Acts…"  
**Claim (Green):** Apocalyptic unveiling (opened heaven, voice, dove “in bodily form”); solidarity with repentant people via baptism; prayer as revelation/commission setting in Luke-Acts.

### C15 — Heavenly voice: Ps 2:7 + Isa 42:1 (+ Gen 22:2); non-adoptionistic Son; Spirit supersedes oil
**Locus:** raw 6264–6269 (slice ll. 264–269)  
**Quote:** "One hears first Ps 2:7… connection was made between “Son of God” and the Davidic throne… “Son of God” can no longer be understood in an adoptionistic sense and where anointing with oil has been superseded by endowment with the Spirit… The second text foregrounded… is Isa 42:1… Finally, we may hear echoes of Gen 22:2…"  
**Claim (Green):** Divine sanction of [[jesus]] as Davidic anointed + Isaianic Servant; boundaries of power = obedience to God’s purpose (what the devil will test).

### C16 — Genealogy: public-service age; “as was thought” of Joseph; Adam son of God = solidarity + crescendo
**Locus:** raw 6273–6287 (slice ll. 273–287)  
**Quote:** "Jesus “was the son (as was thought) of Joseph”… characters within the story will view Jesus as an ordinary human, the son of Joseph, Luke’s auditors should share with the narrator a different (and correct) view… The reference to Adam as son of God presents the divine origin of the human race and indicates Jesus’ solidarity with all humanity… chain of causes… crescendo culminating in the acknowledgment of God as the originator of Jesus’ ancestral line."  
**Claim (Green):** Genealogy legitimates for the story-world while insider audience knows miraculous conception; Jesus not John receives genealogy (superiority).

### C17 — Testing: Spirit-full agency; final competence = positive response to God’s purpose
**Locus:** raw 6316–6321 (slice ll. 316–321)  
**Quote:** "Empowered by the Spirit, Jesus is full of the Spirit, and inspired by the Spirit. His central, active role is therefore fundamentally as God’s agent… 3:21–38… requisite credentials, power, and authority… But these are not enough. They must be matched with Jesus’ positive response to God’s purpose… the testing conducted by the devil seeks specifically to controvert Jesus’ role as Son of God either by disallowing the constraints of that relationship or by rejecting it outright."  
**Claim (Green):** Testing is discernment/actualization of sonship under diabolic reinterpretation; cosmic clash Spirit vs. devil underwrites all later hostility.

### C18 — Israel-in-wilderness typology: Jesus true Son where Israel failed (Deut 6–8)
**Locus:** raw 6323–6337 (slice ll. 323–337)  
**Quote:** "Luke seems deliberately to have drawn together a repertoire of elements from scriptural narration of and reflection on Israel’s wilderness wanderings… Unlike Israel, Jesus proved his fidelity in the wilderness and so is “… presented as the true Son of God, in whom the destiny of Israel was recapitulated and the divine purpose accomplished in that he renders to God the obedience and trust that Israel failed to give.”"  
**Claim (Green; final clause reports scholarly formulation Green adopts):** Representative Israel typology with decisive discontinuity (fidelity vs. rebellion/Isa 63:10).

### C19 — Test 1 (bread): not welfare-king spectacle; trust vs. autonomous use of sonship power
**Locus:** raw 6339–6341 (slice ll. 339–341)  
**Quote:** "Will Jesus follow the leading of the Spirit and manifest unwavering trust in God to supply his needs; or will he relieve his hunger by exercising his power apart from God? The devil does not deny that Jesus is God’s Son, but exploits this status by urging Jesus to use his power in his own way to serve his own ends; he thus reinterprets “Son of God” to mean the opposite of faithful obedience…"  
**Claim (Green):** Singular “bread” and personal famine rule out mass-feeding temptation readings; reply Deut 8:3.

### C20 — Test 2 (kingdoms): devil as world-ruler (irony vs. Caesar); shabby substitute for divine sonship
**Locus:** raw 6343–6353 (slice ll. 343–353)  
**Quote:** "we have been led to believe that “all the world” was under the charge of the Roman emperor (2:1; 3:1). Now… the world of humanity is actually ruled by the devil… The devil proposes to displace God as Jesus’ benefactor… Whatever rule the devil exercises is that allowed him by God… What Jesus is offered, then, is a shabby substitute for the divine sonship that is his by birth."  
**Claim (Green):** Diabolic rule frames Jewish/Gentile darkness; echo of Ps 2:8 / 1:32–33 everlasting kingdom; worship-only-God reply (Deut).

### C21 — Test 3 (temple/Psalm 91): hermeneutical clash; fidelity controls promise; Jerusalem prefigures passion
**Locus:** raw 6355–6358 (slice ll. 355–358)  
**Quote:** "Both quote Scripture; why prefer one reading over the other?… Jesus is radically committed to one aim, God’s eschatological agenda; the devil has an alternative aim… the devil overlooks… that the psalm is addressed to those who through their fidelity to God reside in God’s presence… divine rescue may come through suffering and death and not only before (and from) them."  
**Claim (Green):** Not mere dismissal of devil as unreliable quoter; true issue is competing aims; Jerusalem setting anticipates passion testing (22:3, 28, etc.).

### C22 — Threefold tests encapsulate all ministry testing; devil’s departure = concession of defeat
**Locus:** raw 6359–6362 (slice ll. 359–362)  
**Quote:** "the tests faced here encapsulate all the tests Jesus would meet during the course of his ministry… Jesus can characterize his whole ministry with the language of testing (22:28)… the devil’s departure from Jesus signals the devil’s concession of defeat and concomitant shameful withdrawal."  
**Claim (Green):** Completion of performative competence; hostility throughout is diabolic-backed.

### C23 — 4:14–9:50: programmatic Nazareth then concrete practice; discipleship training; theocentrism
**Locus:** raw 6370–6386 (slice ll. 370–386)  
**Quote:** "4:14–9:50 articulates the pattern of ministry… first by providing a more definitive understanding of the outworking of Jesus’ sonship and empowerment by means of a publicly proclaimed missionary program (4:16–30), then by demonstrating that program in concrete missionary practice… throughout his ministry Jesus is God’s agent… “filled with the power of the Spirit” (4:14–15)."  
**Claim (Green):** Galilee section = actualization stage; proclamation + miracle balanced; wilderness/prayer retreats = ongoing discernment (cf. testing).

### C24 — Nazareth sermon central/programmatic for whole Gospel and Luke-Acts
**Locus:** raw 6452–6455 (slice ll. 452–455)  
**Quote:** "Its central importance for the narrative as a whole is signified by… (1) concrete representation of the ministry… summarized in 4:14–15. (2) first narrated episode of Jesus’ public ministry. (3) … nowhere else does Luke include a report of the content of his [synagogue] teaching… exemplar… (4) … As Son of God, what will Jesus do? In 4:18–19, Jesus interprets his baptism as a Spirit anointing for his mission… (5) Subsequent summaries… refer back to this account (7:21–22; Acts 10:38)."  
**Claim (Green):** 4:16–30 is load-bearing programmatic text for [[jesus]]’ vocation after Spirit anointing/testing.

### C25 — Isaiah mix-text: Isa 61:1–2 + Isa 58:6 “release”; omit “day of vengeance”
**Locus:** raw 6472–6489 (slice ll. 472–489)  
**Quote:** "The bulk of 4:18–19 derives from Isa 61:1–2, but two departures… First, Isa 61:2b, “and the day of vengeance of our God,” has been omitted from Luke 4:19, probably to suppress what would have been taken as a negative aspect… Second, language from Isa 58:6, literally, “to send forth the oppressed in release,” has been added… to draw special attention to the word “release” as a characteristic activity of Jesus’ ministry."  
**Claim (Green):** Structural emphasis: threefold “me”; primary mission “preach good news to the poor”; subordinate infinitives; double ἄφεσις/release.

### C26 — “Poor” = low status honor / outsiders, not only spiritual or cash-poor
**Locus:** raw 6493–6497 (slice ll. 493–497)  
**Quote:** "In that culture, one’s status in a community was not so much a function of economic realities, but depended on a number of elements, including education, gender, family heritage, religious purity, vocation, economics, and so on… “poor” would serve as a cipher for those of low status, for those excluded according to normal canons of status honor… Jesus indicates his refusal to recognize those socially determined boundaries…"  
**Claim (Green):** Holistic outsider definition drives mission; “blind” likewise physical + metaphor of revelation/salvation/inclusion.

### C27 — Release (ἄφεσις): forgiveness/community restoration; anti-Satanic healing; debt/Jubilee
**Locus:** raw 6500–6505 (slice ll. 500–505)  
**Quote:** "Elsewhere in Luke-Acts, “release” is often best translated as “forgiveness”… restoration to or entry into the community… “release” made available via Jesus’ ministry is set in opposition to the binding power of Satan… as “release from debts” (cf. 11:4). This draws our attention to Jubilee legislation (Leviticus 25)—the freeing of slaves, the cancellation of debts, the fallowing of the land, and the returning of all land to its original distribution under Moses… “the year of the Lord’s favor,” borrowed from Isa 61:2."  
**Claim (Green):** Triple construal of release ties [[jubilee]] themes (via Isa 58/61 interpretive tradition) to forgiveness and liberation from diabolic oppression; 4:18–19 = eschatological epoch announcement with Jesus as anointed herald.

### C28 — 11QMelchizedek parallel (reported): shared eschatological Jubilee; differing beneficiaries
**Locus:** raw 6506–6507 (slice ll. 506–507)  
**Quote:** "A comparison of Luke 4:16–30 with 11QMelchizedek is thus interesting for the way both underscore the inauguration of the epoch of salvation and spotlight a messianic figure… Of equal importance… is the way these texts differ… For the Qumranic text, the jubilary message is employed so as to certify how God will deliver God’s people (defined as those of this community), while damning others… Within the Lukan co-text… God’s favor is foregrounded, release is moved very much to the center, and any note of damnation… has been discarded."  
**Claim (Green comparing Qumran):** Shared end-time Jubilee frame; Luke universalizes favor vs. sectarian damnation dualism—yet still paired with salvation-as-reversal and non-universal acceptance (2:34–35; Nazareth rage).

### C29 — “Today” fulfillment: epoch inaugurated in Jesus’ person; demand for hearing/response
**Locus:** raw 6510–6517 (slice ll. 510–517)  
**Quote:** "“Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”… with the onset of Jesus’ ministry the long-awaited epoch of salvation had been inaugurated… He is the one anointed by the Spirit, the herald of good news, the one who brings the new era… “in your hearing”… invites, even demands, response."  
**Claim (Green):** Dual sense of “fulfill” (scriptural hopes + temporal completion); not first dawn (already birth narrative) but public embrace of mission; “today” keyword for Luke-Acts.

### C30 — Nazareth admiration is situational irony: “Joseph’s son” vs. Son of God
**Locus:** raw 6518–6519 (slice ll. 518–519)  
**Quote:** "their response is one of admiration… they would thus see themselves as the immediate beneficiaries of the Lord’s favor, for they claim Jesus as the son of one of our own… we know that their understanding of Jesus is erroneous, for we know that Jesus is Son of God, not son of Joseph; he comes to fulfill the purpose of God, not to be restricted either by the demands of the devil (4:1–13) or, now, by those of his own townspeople."  
**Claim (Green):** Positive-then-violent arc; provincial claim to exclusive favor is obstacle parallel to diabolic restriction of sonship.

### C31 — Prophet maxim + Elijah/Elisha outsiders certify mission and rejection
**Locus:** raw 6521–6554 (slice ll. 521–554)  
**Quote:** "no prophet is accepted in the prophet’s hometown… Elijah was sent… to a widow at Zarephath in Sidon… none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian… With these examples, Jesus underscores that “good news to the poor” embraces the widow, the unclean, the Gentile, those of the lowest status… neither the Scriptures nor the current narrative presents these prophetic figures as programmatically oriented to the Gentiles; nor are they portrayed as having turned their backs on Israel."  
**Claim (Green):** [[elijah]]/[[elisha]] anecdotes = divine mandate to exceptional outsiders (low status), not Israel-rejection program; certifies Jesus as prophet; rage/stoning attempt may evoke Deut 13 false-prophet legislation; escape prefigures passion→resurrection→ongoing mission.

### C32 — Capernaum: release from diabolic power; authority Jesus refused from devil now used vs. evil
**Locus:** raw 6571–6577 (slice ll. 571–577)  
**Quote:** "people who “have a demon” and those who suffer from illness are both oppressed by diabolic forces and both in need of “release.” Hence, the heightened emphasis on “release” noted in Jesus’ citation from Isaiah (Luke 4:18–19) is developed first… in terms of release from diabolic power… the very thing the devil promised to give Jesus, “authority,” has come to Jesus as a consequence of his resisting the devil and operating in the sphere of the Holy Spirit…"  
**Claim (Green):** Teaching and exorcism both “word with authority”; healing painted with exorcism language (rebuke/depart) without equating all illness with possession; Capernaum crowds also try to monopolize Jesus (like Nazareth) without understanding scale of mission.

### C33 — Simon’s mother-in-law: release-healing → service/hospitality as authentic response
**Locus:** raw 6598–6600 (slice ll. 598–600)  
**Quote:** "Luke paints this scene very much as an exorcism… As Jesus “rebuked” the demon… so he “rebukes” this fever… Jesus’ ministry of “release” (4:18–19) has begun to take shape… it also restored this woman to her household. Her response… is one of hospitality and gratitude… Luke regards this as an authentic, positive response…"  
**Claim (Green):** First named household ministry of [[peter-apostle]]’s household; service > mere wonder; pattern for later hospitality motif.

### C34 — Kingdom of God (4:43): new order of release vs. diabolic kingdoms; itinerant necessity
**Locus:** raw 6607–6611 (slice ll. 607–611)  
**Quote:** "“kingdom of God” is associated with the “good news” announced in 4:18–19 and the Spirit-anointed ministry… it connotes a new world order where the demonized, the sick, women, and others living on the margins of society… are embraced… fundamental clash between the kingdoms over which the devil has authority and the authority and power of Jesus—the one intent on the bondage and segregation of persons, the other on release and human wholeness in community."  
**Claim (Green):** Divine necessity (“must”) of itinerancy; kingdom = saving activity + community/practices embodying purpose; wilderness again for vocational clarity against crowd pressure.

### C35 — Call of first disciples: paradigmatic response; “catching people”; leave everything
**Locus:** raw 6630–6709 (slice ll. 630–709)  
**Quote:** "they left everything and followed him… Simon’s obedience and declaration of his sinfulness… contrast both with the earlier “amazement” of the crowds and with the questions and opposition… of the Pharisees… “from now on you will be catching people.”… Disciples will no longer catch dead fish… but will catch people, giving them liberty… Leaving all that has been of value, they will now find their fundamental sense of belonging… in relationship to Jesus…"  
**Claim (Green):** [[peter-apostle]] (with James/John) models correct response; narrative need for active “catching” deferred to Acts; theophanic type-scene ~ Isa 6 (epiphany–reaction–reassurance–commission); “sinner” opens forgiveness/friend-of-sinners trajectory without yet fixing full definition; possessions theme launched (cf. §11).

### C36 — Faith and possessions (aside §11): renunciation, alms, hospitality; wealth masters if not mastered
**Locus:** raw 6620–6629 (slice ll. 620–629)  
**Quote:** "“Although Luke consistently speaks about possessions, he does not speak about possessions consistently.”… Wealth masters if it is not mastered… To share with others, including and especially the poor, is to treat them as within one’s circle of friends, family, and kin… Luke… calls for economic redistribution on behalf of those in need, and for the wealthy to give without using their wealth to gain status or to place others in their debt."  
**Claim (Green; Johnson quoted on inconsistency):** Possessions inseparable from social relations/kinship of kingdom; generalized vs. balanced reciprocity and patronage system critiqued earlier (§10).

### C37 — Leper cleansing: Elisha/Naaman link; boundary-crossing touch; Moses compliance for reentry
**Locus:** raw 6716–6728 (slice ll. 716–728)  
**Quote:** "by focusing so adamantly on the cleansing of a leper, this scene advances the relationship established between Jesus and the prophet Elisha in 4:27… Jesus’ action as deliberate (“stretched out his hand” + “touched”), human contact that violated the law… but also communicated acceptance and reentry… he sends the man to the priest… In relating this account… cleansing… interpreted along the lines of the “release” announced in 4:18–19."  
**Claim (Green):** Social disease of impurity (Lev 13); healing = diabolic-conditioned “departure”; ambiguous re: law (violate contagion rules / keep priestly declaration); word+deed reputation grows; prayer withdrawal continues.

### C38 — Paralytic: faith of “them”; forgiveness = healing moment; Son of Man authority on earth
**Locus:** raw 6736–6759 (slice ll. 736–759)  
**Quote:** "When he saw their faith, he said, “Friend, your sins are forgiven you.”… Jesus’ address… and pronouncement of forgiveness is the healing moment… “so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”… “power of the Lord” is synonymous with “Spirit of the Lord”… the healing of this paralytic is a ministry of “release.”"  
**Claim (Green):** First Pharisees/scribes appear as organized Galilee–Judea–Jerusalem monitors; conflict interludes but healing verifies; “Son of Man” self-reference of singularity not primary identity title; crowd barrier + leadership barrier both overcome; doxology: “incredible things today” echoes 4:21.

### C39 — Levi banquet / table fellowship: call sinners to repentance; boundary expansion
**Locus:** raw 6761–6797 (slice ll. 761–797)  
**Quote:** "“I have come to call not the righteous but sinners to repentance.”… Jesus’ practices at the table… communicate, via deed and word, the nature of his ministry and the concomitant enlargement of the boundaries of God’s people… through Jesus’ dispensing with all varieties of credentials for membership other than repentance… Levi has left everything… reorienting his life completely around God’s purpose… The banquet as a representation of the new community being formed around Jesus."  
**Claim (Green):** Symposium form (host, chief guest, discourse); Pharisees’ purity-table ideology labels “toll collectors and sinners”; Jesus as physician echoes Yahweh-as-healer / Ezek 34 indictment of failed shepherds; “poor” of 4:18 includes these outcasts.

### C40 — Fasting controversy: feast of inaugurated time; bridegroom taken away; piety without justice rejected
**Locus:** raw 6798–6800 (slice ll. 798–800)  
**Quote:** "The thing for which hope is expressed in fasting is already present: “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:21)… Sinners are being called to repentance: This is a time for feasting, not fasting!… veiled anticipation of his death… Then fasting will be appropriate… Jesus’ attitude toward Pharisaical fasting is continuous with the prophetic criticism of fasting… when it was not accompanied by acts of justice and mercy (cf. 3:7–9)."  
**Claim (Green):** Boundary-marking asceticism of John/Pharisee groups vs. Jesus movement; eschatological presence governs practice.

### C41 — New/old garments-wineskins: Jesus = fruition of ancient purpose, not “new religion”
**Locus:** raw 6801–6808 (slice ll. 801–808)  
**Quote:** "it would be difficult to imagine Luke insisting that what Jesus is doing in his ministry is “new.” The burden of the birth narrative, the genealogy, the temptation account, and the inaugural sermon in Nazareth… is that Jesus is doing nothing more than bringing to fruition the ancient purpose of God… Jesus interprets his behaviors… as manifestations of God’s ancient purpose coming to fruition, while the concerns of the Pharisees are rejected not only as innovative but also as quite inconsistent with God’s program."  
**Claim (Green):** Against reading privileging sheer novelty; v. 39 (“old is good”) affirms scriptural antiquity; Marcion’s excision of v. 39 noted as reading affirming old over new.

### C42 — Sabbath grainfields: who interprets God’s will? Son of Man lord of Sabbath
**Locus:** raw 6816–6833 (slice ll. 816–833)  
**Quote:** "Not the Sabbath law per se, but this more fundamental question comes to the fore… Who knows and represents God’s will?… Jesus, in declaring the onset of the eschatological Jubilee (see above on 4:18–19), has made this day (“today,” 4:21) the day for providing for humans… “The Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.”… undercut the utility of Sabbath observance as a boundary-keeping mechanism… and it designates Jesus as God’s authorized agent to determine what was appropriate on the Sabbath."  
**Claim (Green):** Dispute over scribal elaboration (plucking as reaping/threshing etc.), not raw Mosaic ban; David hunger analogy = need + Jesus’ superior scriptural understanding; Sabbath identity-marker (Second Temple) reframed by Jubilee/today logic.

### C43 — Withered hand: save life vs. destroy; Sabbath as day of eschatological restoration
**Locus:** raw 6835–6849 (slice ll. 835–849)  
**Quote:** "is it lawful to do good or to do harm on the sabbath, to save life or to destroy it?… Against these Pharisees and scribes, Jesus refuses to represent Sabbath observance as a litmus test for faithfulness to God. More fundamental for him is God’s design to save… “today,” including the Sabbath day, is the day when divine salvation is available… restores to the sabbath command its profound significance: restoration of human beings in their integrity as part of God’s creation."  
**Claim (Green):** Deliberate confrontation illustrating 6:5 authority; non-life-threatening case still demands “good/save”; leaders’ watching = spying toward formal accusation; fury/incomprehension proleptic of later passion opposition (19:48; 23:34).

### C44 — Galilee cultural map (§10): cities not anti-village polarity; patronage/reciprocity parodied
**Locus:** raw 6390–6408 (slice ll. 390–408)  
**Quote:** "Within Luke’s Galilee… such a [city vs. village] distinction has no place… the city is for Jesus a fundamental focal point of his ministry… Luke’s material is more concerned with the patronal system as such… Jesus’ instruction to give without expectation of return… Distinctions based on social status as defined in the larger world are thus overturned… actualization of God’s redemptive aim as status reversal."  
**Claim (Green):** Against simple urban-elite vs. rural-prophet schema; Jerusalem leaders from outside Galilee carry hostility (5:17); peasant margin, gleaning, toll collectors, kinship boundaries form social backdrop for release ministry.

### C45 — John cycle completion + Jesus’ fivefold readiness = assurance God’s aim will be realized
**Locus:** raw 5635–5637, 5667–5668 (slice ll. 35–37, 67–68)  
**Quote:** "Luke 3:1–4:13, therefore, assures us that Jesus will take up his divine mission and adds to our belief that God’s aim will in fact be realized… Eschatological judgment, with its promise of blessing and woe, and of division, has already begun; the stage is set for the public ministry of God’s agent of salvation, Jesus, the Son of God."  
**Claim (Green):** Preparation section’s narrative function is assurance amid non-guaranteed human response; division already underway before Galilee performance stage.
